title: Cephalopod septa take the form of minimal surfaces like soap films

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Cephalopod septa take the form of minimal surfaces like soap films

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Because a septum is first laid down as an elastic membrane under uniform pressure, it takes the shape of a soap film with the same boundary, a surface of minimal area: spherical in a straight cone with a perpendicular attachment, ellipsoidal with an oblique attachment, and saddle-shaped where the line of attachment is sinuous.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: In all cases, provided only that the membrane be isotropic, the form assumed will be precisely that of a soap-bubble under similar conditions of attachment: that is to say, it will be (with the usual limitations or conditions) a surface of minimal area.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XI, “The Logarithmic Spiral”; topic “Septa of chambered shells”. Scope: septa of nautiloid, orthocone and ammonoid shells

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch11-20: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.75

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Modern CT and numerical geometry permit a direct comparison of observed septa with boundary-matched surfaces. Mechanistic assumptions are not perfectly recoverable, but the core minimal-surface prediction is resolvable from existing data.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Extract septal surfaces and attachment boundaries from 3D shells, solve the corresponding minimal-surface problem, and compare observed curvature and area with minimal, constant-mean-curvature and biomechanical alternatives. Shape classes should track boundary orientation as predicted.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Uniform pressure and isotropic membrane assumptions are not directly recorded.

Fossil deformation and later calcification can alter original septal shape.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.7
analysis feasibility: 0.75
data adequacy: 0.65
data existence: 0.8
operationalizability: 0.85

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Mean curvature of a septal mesh, with the suture as the boundary condition, is a direct test of the soap-film claim, and public CT of chambered shells is sufficient to run it on a real sample. Coverage does not include every septal type, but the spherical, oblique and saddle cases are represented well enough to confirm or refute the geometry. Meshing and curvature are specialist but standard and can be done in weeks to a few months.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: From CT of nautiloid and ammonoid septa, estimate mean curvature given the suture as boundary, and compare spherical, ellipsoidal and saddle cases with the attachment Thompson describes. Near-zero mean curvature supports a minimal surface; systematic mean curvature, or a better fit by a non-minimal shell, refutes it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
A thin elastic membrane under pressure is minimal only under the isotropy and uniform-pressure assumptions.

Downloadable CT is richer for Nautilus and a few ammonoids than for the full range of orthocones and suture types.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
analysis feasibility: 0.6
operationalizability: 0.85
discriminating power: 0.7
data existence: 0.65
data adequacy: 0.55
